title: Review of Redox Chemistry
lead: Electrochemistry is built on reactions in which electrons pass from one substance to another. This section reviews how oxidation numbers keep account of those electrons, in covalent compounds as well as ionic ones, and how the half-reaction method balances the equation for a redox reaction in an acidic or a basic solution.
objectives: Describe defining traits of redox chemistry
Identify the oxidant and reductant of a redox reaction
Balance chemical equations for redox reactions using the half-reaction method
summary_html: Redox reactions are defined by changes in reactant oxidation numbers, and those most relevant to electrochemistry involve actual transfer of electrons. Aqueous phase redox processes often involve water or its characteristic ions, H+ and OH−, as reactants in addition to the oxidant and reductant, and equations representing these reactions can be challenging to balance. The half-reaction method is a systematic approach to balancing such equations that involves separate treatment of the oxidation and reduction half-reactions.

exercises.prompt: The reaction above results when using relatively diluted nitric acid. If concentrated nitric acid is used, nitrogen dioxide is produced instead of nitrogen monoxide. Write a balanced equation for this reaction.

Aqueous permanganate ion may also be reduced using aqueous bromide ion, Br<sup>−</sup>, the products of this reaction being solid manganese(IV) oxide and aqueous bromate ion, BrO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>. Write the balanced equation for this reaction occurring in a basic medium.

Identify each half-reaction below as either oxidation or reduction.
(a) ${\text{Fe}}^{3+}+{\text{3e}}^{\text{−}}\;\longrightarrow \;\text{Fe}$
(b) $\text{Cr}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{Cr}}^{3+}+{\text{3e}}^{\text{−}}$
(c) ${\text{MnO}}_{4}{}^{2−}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{MnO}}_{4}{}^{-}+{\text{e}}^{\text{−}}$
(d) ${\text{Li}}^{\text{+}}+{\text{e}}^{\text{−}}\;\longrightarrow \;\text{Li}$

Identify each half-reaction below as either oxidation or reduction.
(a) ${\text{Cl}}^{\text{−}}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{Cl}}_{2}$
(b) ${\text{Mn}}^{2+}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{MnO}}_{2}$
(c) ${\text{H}}_{2}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{H}}^{\text{+}}$
(d) ${\text{NO}}_{3}{}^{-}\;\longrightarrow \;\text{NO}$

answer.solution: Suggested approach: for each part, assign the oxidation number of the element other than oxygen on both sides of the arrow. An increase in oxidation number is oxidation and a decrease is reduction; as a check, balance the half-reaction for charge and see on which side the electrons appear, products for oxidation and reactants for reduction.

exercises.prompt:
Assuming each pair of half-reactions below takes place in an acidic solution, write a balanced equation for the overall reaction.
(a) $\text{Ca}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{Ca}}^{2+}+{\text{2e}}^{\text{−}},$ ${\text{F}}_{2}+{\text{2e}}^{\text{−}}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{2F}}^{\text{−}}$
(b) $\text{Li}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{Li}}^{\text{+}}+{\text{e}}^{\text{−}},$ ${\text{Cl}}_{2}+{\text{2e}}^{\text{−}}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{2Cl}}^{\text{−}}$
(c) $\text{Fe}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{Fe}}^{3+}+{\text{3e}}^{\text{−}},$ ${\text{Br}}_{2}+{\text{2e}}^{-}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{2Br}}^{-}$
(d) $\text{Ag}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{Ag}}^{\text{+}}+{\text{e}}^{\text{−}},$ ${\text{MnO}}_{4}{}^{-}+{\text{4H}}^{\text{+}}+{\text{3e}}^{\text{−}}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{MnO}}_{2}+{\text{2H}}_{2}\text{O}$

Identify the oxidant and reductant of each reaction of the previous exercise, which asks for these equations to be balanced assuming they occur in an acidic solution.
(a) ${\text{H}}_{2}{\text{O}}_{2}+{\text{Sn}}^{2+}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}+{\text{Sn}}^{4+}$
(b) ${\text{PbO}}_{2}+\text{Hg}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{Hg}}_{2}{}^{2+}+{\text{Pb}}^{2+}$
(c) $\text{Al}+{\text{Cr}}_{2}{\text{O}}_{7}{}^{2−}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{Al}}^{3+}+{\text{Cr}}^{3+}$

answer.solution: Oxidized: (a) Sn<sup>2+</sup>; (b) Hg; (c) Al; reduced: (a) H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>; (b) PbO<sub>2</sub>; (c) ${\text{Cr}}_{2}{\text{O}}_{7}{}^{2−};$ oxidizing agent: (a) H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>; (b) PbO<sub>2</sub>; (c) ${\text{Cr}}_{2}{\text{O}}_{7}{}^{2−};$ reducing agent: (a) Sn<sup>2+</sup>; (b) Hg; (c) Al

exercises.prompt:
Identify the oxidant and reductant of each reaction of the previous exercise, which asks for these equations to be balanced assuming they occur in a basic solution.
(a) ${\text{SO}}_{3}{}^{2−}(aq)+{\text{Cu(OH)}}_{2}(s)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{SO}}_{4}{}^{2−}(aq)+\text{Cu(OH)}(s)$
(b) ${\text{O}}_{2}(g)+{\text{Mn(OH)}}_{2}(s)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{MnO}}_{2}(s)$
(c) ${\text{NO}}_{3}{}^{\text{−}}(aq)+{\text{H}}_{2}(g)\;\longrightarrow \;\text{NO}(g)$
(d) $\text{Al}(s)+{\text{CrO}}_{4}{}^{2−}(aq)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{Al(OH)}}_{3}(s)+{\text{Cr(OH)}}_{4}{}^{\text{−}}(aq)$

answer.solution: Oxidized = reducing agent: (a) ${\text{SO}}_{3}{}^{\text{2−}};$ (b) Mn(OH)<sub>2</sub>; (c) H<sub>2</sub>; (d) Al; reduced = oxidizing agent: (a) Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub>; (b) O<sub>2</sub>; (c) ${\text{NO}}_{3}{}^{\text{−}};$ (d) ${\text{CrO}}_{4}{}^{2−}$

exercises.prompt: Why don’t hydroxide ions appear in equations for half-reactions occurring in acidic solution?

answer.solution: Suggested approach: compare the concentrations of H<sup>+</sup> and OH<sup>−</sup> in an acidic solution, using the ion product of water from the chapter on acid-base equilibria, and ask what would happen to any hydroxide ion formed in a solution that holds an excess of hydrogen ion. The keyed answer to the next exercise makes the same argument for basic solution.

exercises.prompt: Why don’t hydrogen ions appear in equations for half-reactions occurring in basic solution?

answer.solution: In basic solution, [OH−] > 1 $\times$ 10−7 M > [H+]. Hydrogen ion cannot appear as a reactant because its concentration is essentially zero. If it were produced, it would instantly react with the excess hydroxide ion to produce water. Thus, hydrogen ion should not appear as a reactant or product in basic solution.

exercises.prompt: Why must the charge balance in oxidation-reduction reactions?

answer.solution: Suggested approach: recall that electrons are transferred in a redox reaction, never created or destroyed, so every electron lost in the oxidation half-reaction is gained in the reduction half-reaction. Connect this to step 6 of the half-reaction method and to the rule that the sum of oxidation numbers equals the charge on a species.
